newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel willing to move tax reform date if SPD helps.
newsitem.headline: Waigel willing to move tax reform date if SPD helps.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the coalition government could move the date forward of its tax reform plans by one year if the opposition Social Democrats accept his proposals as the basis for negotiations.

Waigel said in a speech to parliament he was willing to start the major tax reform on January 1, 1998 if the SPD was willing to work constructively on plans to cut taxes. SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine called for the tax cuts to take effect in 1998.

"We are prepared to launch the tax reform already on January 1, 1998, but you must be willing to take our suggestions as a basis for negotiations and work together constructively with us in the Bundesrat," Waigel said.

Lafontaine earlier threatened to block the government's tax cutting reform measures in the Bundesrat, or upper house of parliament, in its current form because it would not bring real tax relief to most workers.
He also said the SPD would oppose an increase in the value-added tax (VAT) to finance the income tax cuts.

Waigel said he hoped the SPD offer to advance the date of the reform was serious and not just a cheap tactical trick. He said time was pressing and the SPD would have to refrain from sending the bill to conference committee.
Waigel said the bill needed to be completed by August at the latest if it is going to take effect next January, rather than at the start of 1999 as the government has proposed.

"Everything else would be a cheap offer made without believing in it ever being realised," Waigel said. "You have to say farewell from your blockade tactics if you are willing to work with us constructively."
